specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript defines an extractive variant of multi-document summarization whose output is a concept map (connected graph of concept labels and relation labels taken from source text). It presents a practical pipeline to build a benchmark corpus at previously unattained cluster scale: (1) source selection from an existing DIP web crawl (30 topics, ~40 documents/topic); (2) automatic proposition extraction via Open IE with confidence filtering; (3) an SVM classifier to filter unsuitable tuples; (4) scalable crowdsourced importance annotation via a novel low-context design (Likert and sampled pairwise comparisons aggregated with averages and TrueSkill); (5) expert post-editing of propositions; (6) expert construction of 25-concept connected gold maps (allowing a few synthetic relations); (7) release of baseline system and three automatic evaluation metrics. Empirical evidence reported includes pilot reliability on TAC2008 (Pearson ≈0.8, test-retest ≈0.82 for Likert), in-corpus repeat correlations (≈0.72–0.82), classifier/filter tuning on small labeled sets (500/350 instances), annotation agreement for expert map construction (κ≈0.66–0.70), extraction/filtering statistics (Open IE → ~4137 tuples/topic → filtered to ~1554 usable propositions/topic), crowdsourcing volume/cost ($4.4k), and baseline ablations showing coverage and relation-extraction bottlenecks. Overall, the paper convincingly demonstrates that a pragmatic combination of automated preprocessing, low-context crowdsourcing and expert edits can produce a usable dataset and infrastructure; however, several methodological design choices and the external validity of the proposed evaluation metrics remain partially supported and need clearer quantification and discussion.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: Human note-taking behavior favors concept/relations over full textual summaries → concept maps are a plausible user-facing summary format.
Task definition: Define extractive concept-map-based MDS with size and connectedness constraints to enable (semi-)automatic evaluation.
Scalability challenge: Manual creation for large clusters is infeasible → need automation + crowdsourcing + expert steps.
Extraction: Open IE provides proposition-like tuples; filter by confidence to reduce noise.
Suitability: Not all tuples are map-suitable → train SVM with manual labels to further filter while tuning to avoid false negatives.
Importance scoring: Low-context crowdsourcing (Likert + sampled pairwise/TrueSkill) yields reliable importance estimates per proposition.
Gold construction: Use ranked propositions, expert revision, and expert map assembly (25 concepts, connected), with small allowance for synthetic relations.
Evaluation & baseline: Release baseline and three automatic metrics (strict, METEOR-based, ROUGE-2) and show baseline reveals main bottlenecks (selection, relation extraction).

identified_claims.claim_text: Concept-map-based multi-document summarization is a useful and meaningful variant of MDS that aligns with observed human behavior when organizing information.
evidence: Cites user studies (Chin et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2011) claiming humans note keywords and relations rather than full summaries.
Argues concept maps make relations explicit and support navigation when linked to source locations.
Authors present corpus and baseline to enable research on this task.
uncertainty_flags: No task-based user study in this work demonstrating that concept maps improve real user tasks relative to textual summaries.
Claim of alignment with human behavior is supported by prior user studies but not directly validated for these gold maps.

identified_claims.claim_text: Low-context importance annotation (crowdsourcing scheme scoring context-light propositions) yields reliable importance estimates for propositions across large heterogeneous document clusters.
evidence: Pilot on TAC2008: Likert average worker correlation 0.81; test-retest Pearson 0.82 for Likert.
In-corpus: Likert average agreement 0.80 across topics; repeat correlations ≈0.72–0.73.
Comparison majority agreement ≈0.73 (pilot) and 0.78 (in-corpus).
Extrinsic evaluation: peer summary scores from proposition importance correlate with TAC responsiveness similarly to ROUGE/Pyramid (reported for 3 topics).
uncertainty_flags: Pilot and extrinsic correlations use very small topic samples (3 TAC topics; three repeated in-corpus topics), limiting generality.
Low-context may fail when topic description is insufficient or propositions require document-level qualifiers (authors acknowledge).
Using only top-100 for pairwise comparisons could bias fine-grained ranking.

identified_claims.claim_text: The corpus of 30 topics (≈40 web documents per topic) with gold concept-map summaries can be created efficiently using a pipeline combining Open IE, automated filtering, scalable crowdsourcing, and expert post-editing.
evidence: Describes steps: Open IE extraction (avg 4137 tuples/topic), confidence thresholding tuned on 500 tuples to retain 98.7% of correct extractions in test half; SVM filter trained on 500/350 samples, tuned to avoid false negatives leading to 43% reduction; manual correction of 17k uncertain negatives yielding 955 corrections; crowdsourcing workload (53k Likert + 12k comparison tasks) costing $4,425.45; expert revision and map construction to 25 concepts (avg 0.77 synthetic relations).
Corpus statistics: 30 topics, avg cluster size 97,880 tokens, 25-concept maps, splits provided.
uncertainty_flags: Several thresholds and classifier choices tuned on small labeled samples — potential overfitting or selection bias.
Expert post-editing and allowance for synthetic relations introduce an abstractive component; degree of expert curation is not fully quantified (time, number of edits logged).
Claim of efficiency is relative: $4.4k and non-trivial expert effort were required; full reproducibility depends on providing annotation logs and scripts (authors say resources released).

identified_claims.claim_label: Baseline & metrics as usable starting point
identified_claims.claim_text: The released baseline system and proposed automatic evaluation metrics provide a usable starting point and reveal substantial challenges (notably content selection and relation extraction) for future research.
evidence: Baseline described: NP extraction, merging, relation heuristics, Random Forest importance classifier, heuristic graph pruning.

Reported coverage: extraction covers ~76% of gold concepts; top-25 selection contains only ~17% of gold concepts; final maps have ~17% gold concept coverage; low strict-match scores indicate relation-extraction problems.
Evaluation metrics: strict matching after stemming, METEOR-based fuzzy matching, ROUGE-2 over concatenated propositions, and scripts released.
uncertainty_flags: Metric validity (correlation with human judgments of map quality) is not established on this corpus beyond small pilot; hence 'usable' is plausible but not fully proven.
Baseline is simple; while it surfaces bottlenecks, stronger baselines or ablations using Open IE propositions directly could provide more insights.

strengths.title: Comprehensive, reproducible end-to-end pipeline
strengths.description: The paper presents a full pipeline from raw web clusters to gold concept maps, with explicit steps, parameter choices, and reported intermediate statistics enabling replication.
evidence: Detailed description of extraction, filtering, crowdsourcing, expert revision, and map construction steps (Sections 4.2–4.6).
Reported numbers: average tuples/topic, filtering rates, agreement statistics, crowdsourcing volumes and costs.

strengths.title: Novel crowdsourcing design that scales importance judgments
strengths.description: Low-context Likert plus sampled pairwise annotation (aggregated with TrueSkill) reduces task complexity and worker load while achieving reasonable reliability in pilots and in-corpus repeats.
evidence: Pilot: Likert worker correlation 0.81; test-retest Pearson 0.82. In-corpus: mean Likert agreement 0.80, comparison majority 0.78.
Operational design: grouping 5 propositions per task, payment levels, trap items, worker filters described.

strengths.title: Resource scale and heterogeneity
strengths.description: The released corpus uses large, heterogeneous web clusters (~40 docs/topic; avg cluster 97k tokens) that are larger and more diverse than classic summarization datasets, creating a challenging benchmark.
evidence: Table 2: comparison to DUC/TAC clusters; reported Jensen-Shannon divergence higher than DUC/TAC.
Genre breakdown sample: mixture of articles, blogs, forums, educational material.

concerns.title: Validity of low-context importance across topic types
concerns.description: Low-context annotation assumes that topic descriptions provide enough disambiguating context for workers; this may fail for obscure, technical, or ambiguous topics, biasing importance toward generic topical facts rather than cluster-specific centrality.
evidence: Authors note preliminary tests and caveat that design 'works reasonably well as long as the topic is something the worker can relate to'.
Repeat/pilot reliability uses small topic samples (3 TAC topics; 3 randomly selected in-corpus topics).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add experiments measuring annotation validity on a held-out set of more technical/ambiguous topics (or stratify existing topics by difficulty), include analysis of cases where low-context judgments diverge from document-context judgments, and report human-task outcomes demonstrating practical utility (e.g., user study or extrinsic task with maps).

concerns.title: Dependence on Open IE quality and small tuning samples
concerns.description: Key pipeline steps (confidence thresholding and SVM-based suitability filter) are tuned on small manual samples (500 and 350 instances), raising overfitting/generalization risk and leaving unclear how many important propositions are lost upstream.
evidence: Confidence threshold tuned on 250/250 split to 0.5 retaining 98.7% of correct extractions in the unseen half.
SVM trained on 350 instances, assumed 20% manual verification; classifier filtered 43% of propositions and manual checks corrected 955 of 17k uncertain negatives.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide sensitivity analysis: vary thresholds and retrain SVM with cross-validation; report recall of gold-map propositions w.r.t. original extractions before and after filtering; publish the labeled tuning sets and logs of manual corrections for reproducibility.

concerns.title: Expert post-editing and synthetic relations introduce abstractive components
concerns.description: Although the task is framed as extractive, expert edits (span corrections, conjunction splitting) and allowance of up to three synthetic relations per map introduce abstractive elements not fully quantified, complicating claims of extractiveness and evaluation independence.
evidence: Proposition revision includes breaking conjunctions and span edits; maps may include on average 0.77 synthetic relations.
Reviewer digests note expert interventions were used to correct low-confidence negatives and fix certain tuple types.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify the extent and types of expert edits (counts, examples), log whether final labels appear verbatim in source docs, and annotate maps where synthetic relations occur so downstream evaluations can optionally ignore or treat them separately.

concerns.title: Automatic evaluation metric validity not established
concerns.description: Proposed automatic metrics (strict, METEOR-based, ROUGE-2 on propositions) are plausible, but correlation with human judgments of concept-map quality is not demonstrated on the new corpus beyond small pilots.
evidence: Pilot extrinsic evaluation used TAC2008 peers (3 topics) to show proposition importance correlates with TAC responsiveness; metric-to-human correlation for map-level metrics not reported on corpus.
Prior-stage reviewers flagged limited metric validation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run human evaluations comparing metric scores to human assessments of map usefulness/faithfulness on a representative sample (e.g., 10 maps) and report correlation coefficients and qualitative failure cases; provide guidance on when to prefer strict vs fuzzy metrics.

concerns.title: Operational design choices (25 concepts, connectedness) constrain outcomes
concerns.description: Design choices such as fixed 25-concept size and requiring connected graphs strongly shape map structure; alternative constraints might produce different, possibly more useful summaries. The paper doesn't explore these design trade-offs.
evidence: Authors justify 25 concepts as recommended maximum and require connectedness; annotator notes balancing importance vs connections.
Shared analysis flag notes connectedness and size are design choices not explored.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include an ablation or discussion showing how map properties and coverage change with different size/connectivity budgets (e.g., 15, 25, 35 concepts; allowing disconnected components), or at least discuss rationale and potential effects more explicitly.

Open IE and SVM filter thresholds were tuned on small labeled samples; risk of overfitting and lost important propositions exists.
Expert interventions (revision, synthetic relations) create partial abstraction; the extractive claim depends on degree of editing.

Low coverage of gold concepts in top-25 selection (17%) might indicate either that the classifier/feature set is insufficient or that the concept distribution is very long-tailed and that alternative selection paradigms (graph-based, cluster-aware ranking) are needed.

Expert edits could be doing a large fraction of the heavy lifting, so the produced gold maps may reflect expert summarization strategy as much as crowd consensus; the resource is still valuable but has a mixed provenance.
transparency_notes: The pipeline steps, thresholds, and counts are reported in detail, which aids reproducibility; however, the labeled tuning datasets (500/350 instances), the manual correction logs (17k checked, 955 corrected), and the precise expert edit records should be released alongside the corpus for full transparency.
Costs and worker filters are reported; more details about expert time per topic and examples of synthetic relations would clarify the true annotation cost/effort.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While the pipeline and low-context annotation scheme appear novel relative to prior corpora and concept-map work, novelty alone does not guarantee validity; the main risks are methodological (annotation context limits, extraction/filtering dependence) rather than conceptual.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If topic descriptions are clear and about general-interest subjects, low-context judgments will reliably reflect importance and produce high-quality maps.
If Open IE recall on proposition-worthy spans is sufficiently high for the domain, filtering and crowdsourcing will retain most summary-worthy propositions so experts only perform light editing.

If the community adopts the released metrics and tools and researchers validate and extend metric–human correlations on the corpus, the resource will catalyze follow-up work addressing relation extraction and selection bottlenecks.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Extends summarization benchmarks by producing a sizeable, heterogeneous dataset for a non-textual extractive output (concept maps) and introduces a scalable importance-annotation technique; this is a meaningful step beyond existing single-document or small-cluster concept-map datasets.
evidence: 30 topics × ~40 docs/topic, larger clusters than DUC/TAC and Villalon corpus; low-context annotation design and reported agreement metrics.
uncertainty_flags: Dependence on extraction/filtering and limited metric validation lowers immediate reusability until tuning sets and logs are released.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Defining extractive concept-map MDS as an evaluation-ready task with a released corpus could shift some research from text-generation-centric summaries to structured, navigable outputs; however practical utility for end-users is not demonstrated here.
evidence: Task framing, extractive constraint, and release of baseline/eval scripts make the task operational.
uncertainty_flags: No user studies or task-based evaluations to show concept maps outperform or complement textual summaries in real use.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects uncertainties about generalization of low-context annotation and the small tuning samples for extraction/filtering; upper bound reflects the substantial, well-documented empirical work, reproducible pipeline, and clear reporting that support many claims. The interval expresses moderate-to-high confidence in the core contributions (resource and annotation design) but lower confidence in broader validity claims (metric alignment, generalization to all topic types).

consensus_findings: The manuscript defines an extractive concept-map variant of multi-document summarization and provides a coherent end-to-end pipeline (Open IE extraction -> filtering -> low-context crowdsourced importance annotation -> expert revision -> gold map construction).

A new corpus of 30 topics (~40 heterogeneous web documents per topic) with gold concept maps was produced and documented; cluster size and heterogeneity are substantially larger than classic MDS corpora (DUC/TAC).

The low-context crowdsourcing design (Likert + sampled pairwise with TrueSkill) yields internally consistent importance scores with repeat correlations typically around 0.7–0.82 in pilots and in-corpus repeats.

Open IE + automated filtering is an effective pragmatic starting point but is a critical dependency: extraction quality and filtering choices materially shape candidate propositions and require nontrivial manual correction.

A simple baseline and three proposition-level automatic metrics (strict match, METEOR-based fuzzy match, ROUGE-2 over propositions) are provided and show that content selection and relation extraction are major bottlenecks for current automated systems.
disagreements: Extent to which low-context importance judgments generalize: some reviewers view the pilot and in-corpus repeat reliability as promising evidence of generalizability, while others emphasize that validation is limited (small number of pilot topics, likely topical familiarity bias) and call for expert vs. crowd comparisons on a broader, more technical subset.

Degree to which the corpus creation is truly 'efficient' and scalable: some reviewers treat reported crowdsourcing cost as evidence of efficiency, whereas others stress that expert time/corrections (17k negative inspections, proposition revision, synthetic relations) were substantial but not quantified and may limit scalability.

Validity and sufficiency of the proposed automatic evaluation metrics: reviewers agree metrics are a reasonable starting point but disagree on how much to rely on them before performing metric–human correlation studies; some recommend immediate metric validation as essential, others view it as next-step work.

Interpretation of high annotation agreement: some reviewers attribute it to robust task design, others caution that agreement may reflect topic familiarity and prevalence of easily judged, generic facts rather than nuanced, document-specific importance.
uncertainty_hotspots: Low-context annotation external validity: performance on obscure, technical, or ambiguous topics (worker familiarity effects and topic-description sensitivity) is not yet established.

Open IE extraction and filtering: thresholds and SVMs were tuned on relatively small labeled samples (≈500 and ≈350 instances), raising risks of overfitting and systematic omission of important proposition types.

Expert intervention magnitude: the amount, kinds, and time-cost of expert edits (manual corrections of filtered items, proposition revisions, synthetic relations) are incompletely quantified and could materially affect dataset provenance and reproducibility.

Automatic metric validity: correlation between the proposed proposition-based metrics and human judgments of map-level quality (coverage, coherence, usefulness) across the new heterogeneous corpus is not demonstrated.

Pipeline-induced reference bias: gold maps were produced from crowd-ranked and pipeline-filtered propositions (experts worked from a preselected top set), creating potential circularity between upstream pipeline choices and final gold references.
model_diversity_effects: Structure analysts emphasize internal logical coherence and pipeline consistency, highlighting that multiple validation checkpoints are present but flagging pipeline sensitivity to initial extraction errors.

Methodology auditors focus on reproducibility and validity: they request release of tuning sets, classifier artifacts, and explicit accounting of expert labor and manual corrections to assess scalability and replicability.

Novelty assessors (incremental and disruptive) stress different impact axes: some see the dataset as meaningful incremental infrastructure work (large, heterogeneous corpus), others as potentially disruptive (reframing MDS outputs), with both contingent on metric and usability validation.

Claim verifiers consolidate empirical evidence and uncertainties, stressing that many empirical numbers are internally consistent but that extrapolation beyond reported topics and settings is limited by small tuning/pilot samples and opaque expert steps.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a substantial resource/engineering contribution that meaningfully extends existing benchmarks, but one that requires targeted additional validations and transparency before being used as a canonical evaluation standard. Center editorial decisions on whether the authors are willing to (a) expand or clearly qualify evidence about low-context annotation generalization, (b) provide full reproducibility artifacts (tuning sets, corrected negatives, trained classifiers, exact topic list/URLs, HIT templates, and random seeds), (c) quantify expert labor and edits, and (d) run modest metric–human correlation experiments (or commit to making the dataset available conditional on those validations). If the authors accept and address these transparency and validation tasks (or clearly document them in the released package and paper appendix), the resource is likely to be of high community value. Maintain the editor's central role in setting the scope of required revisions: request concrete artifact release, defined additional experiments (see Author Guidance), and explicit discussion of residual limitations and intended use-cases of the corpus.
meta_review.author_guidance: Address the major uncertainty hotspots and transparency gaps: (1) provide and publish the small labeled sets used for Open IE threshold tuning (the 500 sample split), the SVM training/validation set, and the list/log of manually corrected negatives (including per-topic counts and examples); (2) report expert annotation effort in person-hours per topic, number of experts, and representative examples of proposition edits and synthetic relations (annotated edit logs); (3) perform and report at least small-scale validation experiments: (a) compare low-context importance scores against expert document-context importance judgments on a representative subset of 6–10 topics (including at least some technical/obscure topics), and (b) run a metric–human correlation study for the proposed automatic metrics on a held-out set of system-generated maps (e.g., 50 comparisons rated by independent humans for coverage/coherence/usefulness), reporting correlation coefficients and confidence intervals; (4) explicitly discuss the consequences of constructing gold maps from pipeline outputs (selection bias) and provide an analysis contrasting a small set of expert-constructed-from-documents maps with pipeline-driven gold maps to quantify divergence; (5) release all annotation guidelines, HIT templates, TrueSkill settings, classifier code, model files and seeds, and the exact list of chosen DIP topics/URLs. If resource constraints prevent running all suggested experiments, clearly state limitations and provide prioritized roadmap and timelines for planned validations.
transparency_report: Reported: crowdsourcing volumes, total spend ($4,425.45), many pipeline thresholds and intermediate counts (tuples/topic, filtered counts, agreement stats).

Missing or insufficiently reported artifacts: the small labeled tuning datasets used for Open IE thresholding (the 500-sample split) and SVM training (≈350 instances), the list of manually corrected negative propositions (17k checked, 955 corrected) with per-topic breakdown, and expert edit logs showing exact proposition revisions and synthetic relation insertions.

Reproducibility artifacts requested: exact list of 30 selected DIP topics and URLs, HIT/task templates and qualification filters, worker trap-item definitions, random seeds and data splits, trained classifier model files and training scripts (SVM and Random Forest), and code for TrueSkill aggregation and sampling strategy.

Documentation gaps: explicit per-topic expert person-hours, number of expert annotators and their qualifications, and documentation of how topic descriptions were composed/selected (to permit sensitivity analyses).
epistemic_limits: Evidence for low-context annotation reliability is based on small pilot topic samples and in-corpus repeats; thus claims about generalizability to all topic types (especially niche/technical) are uncertain.
Open IE and filtering evaluations were tuned on small manually labeled sets; confidence about preserved recall of important propositions outside the tuning distribution is limited.

Gold references are not fully independent of the pipeline that produced candidates (experts worked from pre-ranked proposition pools), limiting the epistemic independence of evaluation: poor system outputs that differ from pipeline priors may be penalized beyond intrinsic quality differences.

Automatic metrics are proposition-lexical-overlap oriented; without demonstrated correlations to human judgments on this corpus, their capacity to measure map utility or structural fidelity is provisional.

Reviewer syntheses rely on reported manuscript numbers and artifacts made available for review; any undisclosed changes, omitted logs, or inaccuracies in reporting would alter assessments and recommended follow-up experiments.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript defines extractive concept-map multi-document summarization and delivers a pragmatic end-to-end pipeline (Open IE extraction → confidence/SVM filtering → low-context crowdsourced importance annotation → expert revision → 25-concept connected gold maps). It releases a 30-topic corpus (≈40 heterogeneous web docs/topic), a simple baseline, and three proposition-level automatic metrics. Empirical evidence includes pilot and in-corpus agreement/correlation statistics for low-context annotation (Pearson ≈0.7–0.82), Open IE extraction and filtering counts and tuning on small labeled samples, crowdsourcing volume/cost reporting, and baseline analyses showing extraction and content-selection as main bottlenecks.
strengths: End-to-end, well-documented pipeline with intermediate diagnostics (extraction counts, filtering rates, agreement stats) that aids reproducibility.
Novel, pragmatic crowdsourcing design (low-context Likert + sampled pairwise with TrueSkill) that scales importance annotation and shows consistent internal reliability in pilots and repeats.

A sizable, heterogeneous corpus (30 topics, ~40 web documents/topic) markedly larger and more diverse than classic MDS corpora, together with baseline code and evaluation scripts to bootstrap research.
limitations: Limited validation of low-context importance generalization: pilot and repeat analyses focus on a small set of topics (e.g., 3 TAC topics in pilot) and on DIP topics likely to be worker-relatable; robustness for obscure/technical topics or where document-level qualifiers are needed is untested.

Dependence on Open IE and small tuning samples: confidence-thresholding and SVM filtering were tuned on relatively small manual sets (~500 and ~350 instances), and substantial manual inspection/corrections (17k negatives inspected, 955 corrected) were required — raising reproducibility and selection-bias concerns.

Insufficient quantification of expert effort and edits: expert post-editing (proposition revisions, conjunction splitting, synthetic relations) materially affects gold maps but per-topic person-hours, edit logs, and counts/types of edits are not fully reported.

Automatic evaluation metric validity is provisional: the proposed strict/METEOR/ROUGE-2 proposition metrics have limited demonstrated correlation with human judgments on the new heterogeneous corpus; metric–human validation is recommended.
open_questions: Please provide or summarize the labeled samples used to tune extraction/filtering (the 500-sample Open IE threshold set and the ≈350 SVM training instances) and the list or per-topic counts of manually corrected negatives (the 17k inspected, 955 corrected) so others can reproduce and analyze selection bias.

Can the authors report expert annotation effort explicitly (number of expert annotators, qualifications, and average person-hours per topic for proposition revision and final map construction) and publish anonymized edit logs showing which propositions were changed/merged/synthesized?

How do low-context importance scores compare to document-context (full-context) importance judgments from domain experts across a representative subset (6–10) that includes at least some technical/obscure topics? Please provide correlation and example failure modes.

What are the correlations (Pearson/Spearman and confidence intervals) between the three proposed automatic metrics and independent human ratings of map-level quality (coverage, coherence, usefulness) on a held-out set of system-generated maps (suggested sample: ~50 comparisons)?
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper provides a coherent, reproducible pipeline and a novel, useful resource: a 30-topic, large-cluster corpus of concept-map summaries plus baseline code and evaluation scripts.
There is agreement that low-context crowdsourcing is an innovative, scalable annotation design with encouraging internal reliability numbers.
Reviewers concur that Open IE extraction and the subsequent filtering steps are critical dependencies that materially shape candidate propositions and require careful documentation.
Everyone accepts that baseline experiments highlight content selection and relation extraction as key bottlenecks for automated systems on this task.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers interpret the pilot/in-corpus agreement figures as reasonable evidence of generalizability for low-context annotation; others see those figures as insufficient and require expert vs. crowd comparisons on more diverse topics.

There is divergence about whether current metric proposals are adequate as-is: all see them as starting points, but some expect immediate metric–human validation to be required while others consider it reasonable follow-up work.

Assessments differ on how problematic the expert interventions are: some view the manual edits as acceptable pragmatic steps, others worry they introduce nontrivial abstraction and potential circularity between pipeline outputs and gold maps without quantified edit logs.
uncertainty_snapshot: External validity of low-context annotations for non-general-interest topics remains uncertain.
Extent to which small tuning sets (500/350 samples) generalize across diverse web genres and whether important proposition types are systematically lost by extraction/filtering is unclear.
Degree to which expert edits change the extractiveness and independent validity of gold maps is not quantified.
Metric–human alignment for proposition-graph outputs on heterogeneous clusters is provisional until correlation analyses are provided.
source_trace: Pilot and in-corpus low-context annotation reliability statistics reported in manuscript Sections 3.2 and 4.4 (TAC2008 pilot: Likert Pearson ≈0.81; in-corpus Likert agreement ≈0.80; repeat correlations ≈0.72–0.82).
Open IE extraction and threshold tuning described in Section 4.2 (avg ~4137 tuples/topic; confidence threshold tuned on 500 manually labeled tuples; post-filtering ≈1554 usable propositions/topic).
SVM suitability filtering, manual inspection of uncertain negatives (17k inspected, 955 corrected) and classifier training details reported in Section 4.3.
Crowdsourcing volume and cost numbers stated in Section 4.4 (≈53k scoring + 12k comparison tasks; total spend $4,425.45).

Expert proposition revision and map construction procedures and inter-annotator agreement statistics are in Sections 4.5–4.6 (25-concept maps, average synthetic relations ≈0.77, reported κ and selection/join agreement figures).
Baseline pipeline and metric definitions (strict matching, METEOR-based partial match, ROUGE-2 over propositions) and bottleneck analyses are in Section 6.

transparency_notes: Manuscript is strong in reporting many intermediate counts, thresholds, crowdsourcing volumes, and aggregate agreement statistics. Missing for full reproducibility are the small labeled tuning datasets (Open IE 500-sample split; SVM ≈350 instances), the explicit list and per-topic breakdown of manually corrected negatives (17k inspected, 955 corrected), expert person-hour accounting and edit logs for proposition revisions/synthetic relations, precise HIT templates/qualification filters, TrueSkill settings and sampling strategy, trained classifier/model files and seeds, and the exact list of 30 DIP topic URLs. Releasing these artifacts alongside the corpus will materially improve reproducibility and enable the community to assess selection biases.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Handle this submission as a substantial resource-engineering contribution that merits conditional acceptance contingent on improved transparency and targeted validation. Require the authors to (a) release the tuning/labeled sets and manual-correction logs (or provide them as supplementary materials with per-topic breakdowns), (b) report expert annotator time and edit logs (examples of proposition edits and synthetic relations), and (c) run or report small, focused validation studies: an expert vs. low-context importance comparison on a representative subset (6–10 topics including technical/obscure topics) and a metric–human correlation study on a held-out sample of system-generated maps. If the authors provide these artifacts and/or experiments or clearly document a prioritized plan and timeline for releasing them, the resource will be suitable for broad community use. If constrained, require clear, explicit caveats in the paper about generalization limits, pipeline dependence, and gold-map provenance.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and the released resource, please (1) publish the small labeled datasets used for Open IE threshold tuning (the 500-sample split) and for SVM training/validation (~350 instances), plus the list/log of manually corrected negatives with per-topic counts and representative examples; (2) report expert annotation labor: number of experts, qualifications, and average person-hours per topic, and provide anonymized edit logs showing proposition edits, mergers, splits and synthetic relations; (3) run and report two modest validation experiments: (a) compare low-context crowd importance scores with document-context expert importance judgments on 6–10 diverse topics (report correlations, disagreement cases, and examples), and (b) perform a metric–human correlation study for the three proposed metrics using independent human ratings of coverage/coherence/usefulness over ~50 map comparisons (report Pearson/Spearman and 95% CIs); (4) discuss and quantify the dependence of final gold maps on upstream pipeline choices (provide one or two topics where experts produce maps directly from documents and compare to pipeline-driven gold maps); (5) release all annotation guidelines, HIT templates, TrueSkill and sampling parameter settings, model training scripts and weights (SVM and RF), random seeds, and the exact list of 30 DIP topics/URLs. If some items cannot be released, document the reason and provide detailed summaries and representative samples instead.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
Summary:
The paper defines an extractive concept-map MDS task and presents a complete pipeline (Open IE → filtering → low-context crowdsourcing → expert revision → gold maps), producing a 30-topic, heterogeneous corpus, baseline, and three proposition-level metrics. Empirical reporting (extraction counts, filtering rates, crowdsourcing volumes/costs, agreement/correlation statistics) is detailed and supports the claim that a pragmatic combination of automation, crowd microtasks, and expert editing can produce usable gold maps at this scale.

Strengths:
- End-to-end, transparent pipeline with many intermediate diagnostics and aggregate statistics to guide replication.
- Scalable, novel crowdsourcing design (low-context Likert + sampled pairwise) with encouraging internal reliability measures.
- Resource scale and heterogeneity exceed classic MDS corpora; release of baseline and scripts lowers barrier for follow-up work.

Limitations:
- Low-context annotation generalization is insufficiently validated for obscure/technical topics — reported pilots/repeats are limited in topic breadth.
- Heavy dependence on Open IE plus small-sample tuned filters; manual inspection/corrections (17k checked) indicate nontrivial expert involvement that is not fully quantified.
- Expert post-editing and allowance for synthetic relations introduce mild abstraction; extent and effect on extractiveness and evaluation independence are not fully documented.
- Proposed automatic metrics lack broad metric–human correlation validation on the new heterogeneous corpus.

Open Questions (requests for clarification/experiments):
1) Provide the 500-sample Open IE tuning set and ≈350 SVM training instances and the list/log of manually corrected negatives with per-topic counts to allow replication and bias analysis.  
2) Report expert annotator details: number, qualifications, and average person-hours per topic for proposition revision and map assembly; provide anonymized edit logs showing types and frequencies of edits and synthetic relations.  
3) Compare low-context crowd importance scores with document-context expert importance judgments on a representative subset (6–10 topics including technical/obscure cases) and report correlations and example divergences.  
4) Provide metric–human correlation results for the three proposed metrics on a held-out set of system-generated maps (suggested ≈50 comparisons) and report correlation coefficients with confidence intervals.

Transparency:
The manuscript already reports many useful figures (counts, thresholds, costs, aggregated agreement stats). To reach reproducibility and to give the community confidence, release the small tuning datasets, manual correction logs, annotator edit logs, HIT templates/qualification settings, TrueSkill and sampling parameters, trained model files and seeds, and the exact list of selected DIP topics/URLs. If any artifacts cannot be released, provide detailed descriptive statistics and representative examples instead.

Strengths:
- The review pipeline identified specific strengths, but they should be validated against the cited evidence.

Limitations:
- The current evidence base may be incomplete for some claims.
- Some findings remain sensitive to corpus coverage and retrieval quality.

Open Questions:
- Which claims most depend on assumptions that are not directly tested?
- Which revisions would most improve the paper's evidentiary grounding?

Transparency:
- This synthesis preserves disagreement and uncertainty rather than collapsing them into a score.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects strong internal reporting (pipeline steps, counts, agreement statistics) which supports the core contribution (a scalable pipeline and released resource). Lower bound accounts for uncertainties around generalization of low-context annotation to obscure topics, small tuning samples for extraction/filtering, and incomplete quantification of expert edits and metric validation. Upper bound reflects the quality of documentation and the pragmatic value of the released corpus and tooling if the transparency gaps are addressed.
